findings.claim: The new attribute is placed on the user-declared partial resolver class (`partial class <ResolverName>`). If a user has already put `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on their own `[GeneratedMessagePackResolver] partial class MyResolver` declaration, which is the obvious workaround for this issue, the merged type now carries the attribute twice. `ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` has AllowMultiple=false, so this raises CS0579 (duplicate attribute) and code that compiled on base stops compiling. CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:7 emits the same attribute on the user's partial composite resolver and breaks the same way.

receipt_plan.detail: Run ExcludeFromCodeCoverageReceiptTests.UserAnnotatedResolver_DoesNotProduceDuplicateAttribute. It runs MessagePackGenerator on a source whose resolver is already marked [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] and asserts the output compilation has no CS0579. It passes on base and fails on head.

findings.claim: The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` suppresses the attribute when the consuming project targets netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` exists on both: netstandard2.0, and .NET Framework 4.0+ where it allows AttributeTargets.Class. Generated formatters and resolvers in those very common target frameworks therefore stay undecorated, so the requirement 'all generated code is decorated' is not met there, even though emitting the attribute would compile.

receipt_plan.detail: Run ExcludeFromCodeCoverageReceiptTests.NetStandard20Consumer_ResolverIsStillExcludedFromCoverage. It runs the generator with preprocessor symbol NETSTANDARD2_0 and asserts the generated resolver type carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute. It fails on head.
